title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) versus \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)
formal: Is \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family \(f=(f_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\})\) in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) such that for every fixed depth \(d\ge 1\), exponent \(k\ge 1\), and constant \(M\ge 1\), there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing \(f_{n}\) exactly has size greater than \(M(n+1)^{k}\)?
definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\), optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than \(m/2\) inputs equal 1. \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) consists of all families with such circuits of size \(M(n+1)^{k}\) and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size \(M(n+1)^{k}\), and depth at most \(b \log _{2}(n+1)\), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subsetneq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\) or \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}=\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) for the nonuniform families defined here. Strictness requires a single \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family with no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family; equality requires that every \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family admit such a family.
why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.

importance.reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.

progress.text: Hesse, Allender, and Barrington place division and iterated multiplication in DLOGTIME-uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\), demonstrating the arithmetic power already available at constant depth.

Chen and Tell show how improvements in the depth dependence of superlinear wire lower bounds for certain \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)-complete problems would yield superpolynomial \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) lower bounds.
Dawar and Evans characterize uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) with typed monoids and unary generalized quantifiers. The containment comparison remains open.

Chen, Tal, and Wang prove superquadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two weighted threshold circuits for an \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) function; the result does not supply an \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) separation against every constant depth.

status_note: The source and subsequent-work checks on 11 September 2026 found no equality or separation of these nonuniform classes. The 2026 depth-two result concerns a function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) and polynomial circuit size; the typed-monoid result concerns uniform classes. These conclusions have different quantifiers and models from the target.

context_blocks.text: The two models trade different resources. A majority gate can aggregate arbitrarily many bits in one step, whereas a binary Boolean gate sees only two. \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) permits logarithmically many layers of binary computation. A majority of polynomially many bits can itself be computed by a polynomial-size logarithmic-depth Boolean circuit, so a constant number of majority layers gives \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\subseteq \mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The open issue is whether counting in a fixed number of layers can also replace every logarithmic-depth computation.

Arithmetic tasks are an instructive warning against judging depth from familiar sequential algorithms. Hesse, Allender, and Barrington prove that integer division and iterated multiplication have even DLOGTIME-uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) circuits. A binary long-division procedure takes many dependent steps, but that procedure does not establish a lower bound on all circuits for division. These arithmetic problems therefore cannot serve as the missing separation.

There are concrete complete problems on the \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) side. Evaluating a Boolean formula, and evaluating a product of elements of the fixed permutation group \(S_{5}\), capture \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) under very simple reductions. \(S_{5}\) consists of the 120 permutations of five objects, with permutation composition as its operation. Chen and Tell study these complete problems in their lower-bound amplification results.

Chen and Tell prove a conditional amplification theorem connecting certain mildly superlinear wire lower bounds to a separation of the full classes. Its hypothesis imposes a specific quantitative dependence on circuit depth. Thus a lower bound proved only at one fixed depth, or with an insufficient exponent at growing constant depths, is a different statement from their theorem’s hypothesis and from the conjecture here.

Dawar and Evans give an algebraic characterization of uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) using typed monoids in FSTTCS 2025, extending earlier work on uniform \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). Typed monoids allow infinite algebraic structures while restricting recognition through finitely many types. This supplies another mathematical language in which to compare the classes. Their theorem is a characterization, not a separation, and its uniform scope must be kept distinct from this card’s formulation.

Chen, Tal, and Wang’s 2026 preprint proves \(n^{2.5- \varepsilon}\) gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits computing a function in \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\). Here \(E^{\mathrm{NP}}\) allows deterministic time \(2^{O(n)}\) with an NP oracle. A linear-threshold gate tests a weighted sum, while this card fixes unweighted majority gates. More decisively, the result treats one depth, a polynomial size bound, and a hard function not shown to belong to \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The target here concerns an \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) family against every fixed depth and every polynomial size bound.

category_assignment.reason: TC⁰ versus NC¹ asks for separation of major nonuniform circuit classes. Preserve its approved computational/circuit complexity placement when the detailed formulation introduces Boolean function families.

sentences: TC0 circuits use a constant number of layers of powerful majority gates.
NC1 circuits use logarithmically many layers of ordinary bounded-input Boolean gates.
The question asks whether the former nonuniform class is strictly weaker than the latter.
Many arithmetic tasks already fit in TC0, so their familiar sequential implementations do not provide separating examples.
The project seeks a function whose nested logical dependencies cannot be compressed into a fixed-depth network even when each gate can aggregate many inputs at once.
